opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the two adoption curves look pretty different, for understandable reasons.

On the patient side, adoption has been surprisingly fast and largely bottom-up. People already turn to the internet when they have a health question, whether it's a new symptom, a confusing lab result, or trying to understand what their doctor told them in a rushed fifteen-minute visit. AI models fit naturally into that existing behavior. They're available at 2 a.m., they're patient, you can ask follow-up questions, and they can explain things in plain language tailored to your situation. So for a lot of people, the alternative isn't a world-class physician on call. It's a search engine, a forum, or nothing at all. Measured against that baseline, the value is immediately obvious, and people just start using it.

Clinicians are in a different position. They carry professional and legal responsibility for outcomes, they work inside institutions with procurement processes, privacy requirements, and EHR integrations, and they've been burned before by technology that promised to save time and ended up adding clicks. So their bar is understandably higher. They want evidence that a tool is accurate in their specific setting, that it fits into the workflow rather than sitting beside it, and that it actually reduces their burden. That said, we've seen real traction where those conditions are met. Ambient documentation is the clearest example, because it addresses a pain point every doctor feels, and the value is easy to verify. Clinicians are also increasingly using models informally as a second opinion or a quick reference, often ahead of official institutional adoption.

The way I think about it is that the two are complementary, and the interesting future lies where they meet. Patients will arrive at appointments better informed, sometimes having already worked through their questions with an AI. That changes the conversation. Ideally it makes visits more collaborative and frees doctors to focus on judgment, relationships, and the hard cases. But it also raises real questions we have to take seriously: how do we make sure what patients get is safe and calibrated, knowing when to say "you need to see someone in person"? And how do we build trust on the clinician side so that AI-informed patients are seen as an asset, not a nuisance?

So the short version: patients adopt because the counterfactual is often so poor, and clinicians adopt when the evidence and the workflow fit are there. A lot of the work for those of us building these systems is earning trust on both fronts at the same time.

r001.rationale: It contrasts patients’ “surprisingly fast” adoption with clinicians’ higher adoption bar and says clinicians adopt when evidence and workflow fit are in place.

r002.rationale: It says patients may arrive having used AI, but does not state that physicians first learn about AI through those patients.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting asymmetry, and I think it comes down to the fact that patients and doctors are facing completely different incentive structures and different starting points.

On the patient side, the adoption has been kind of remarkable, and honestly a little ahead of where I think a lot of us in the field expected. People are already going to these models with their health questions in huge numbers. And I think the reason is pretty simple: the status quo for most patients is really bad. You have a symptom, you're worried, and your options are to wait two weeks for an appointment, go to urgent care, or type it into a search engine and get a page of ads and terrifying worst-case scenarios. A model that will actually engage with your specific situation, ask follow-up questions, explain things in plain language, and do it at 2 AM for free, that's just a dramatically better experience than what was available. So the bar is low and the value is immediate. Patients don't need the model to be a perfect clinician. They need it to be better than nothing, and often better than Dr. Google, and it clearly is.

Doctors are in a totally different position. They already have the expertise, so the incremental value of the model as a knowledge source is lower, and the cost of being wrong is much higher for them professionally. There's liability, there's workflow integration, there's the fact that most of their day isn't actually the hard diagnostic reasoning that makes for a nice benchmark. It's documentation, prior auths, inbox messages, coordination. So the places where we've seen real clinician adoption are things like ambient scribing and drafting responses to patient messages, where the model is removing drudgery rather than trying to be the decision-maker. That's where the trust gets built, and I think the more substantive clinical use follows from that, but it's a slower path and it should be.

The other thing I'd say is that these two things interact. As patients come in having already had a conversation with a model, that changes the dynamic in the exam room. The doctor is now reacting to what the patient brings in, and I think that's going to pull clinician adoption forward in a way that's less about the health system deciding and more about meeting patients where they already are.

r001.rationale: The response describes patient adoption as remarkable and ahead of expectations, while characterizing clinician adoption as slower.

r002.rationale: It says patients’ model conversations change the exam-room dynamic and may pull clinician adoption forward, but does not state that many physicians first learn about AI through patients.

astra-6.text:
I think patients and doctors have pretty different adoption dynamics. For a patient, the alternative to asking an AI often isn’t asking a doctor—it’s searching online, asking a friend, or sitting with uncertainty until an appointment. So even a system with limitations can be useful for explaining a medical term, helping you organize your symptoms, or figuring out what questions to ask. And it’s available whenever you need it.

For doctors, the comparison is different. They already have expertise, and they’re operating within a workflow where mistakes have consequences and they’re accountable for the care they provide. A tool has to do more than produce an impressive answer. It has to fit into that workflow, have access to the relevant information, and save time after you account for checking its work.

So I’d distinguish willingness to try something from willingness to delegate to it. A patient might readily use AI to understand their health without trusting it to make a treatment decision. A doctor might happily use it to draft a note while being much more cautious about its clinical recommendations. Adoption isn’t one switch—it depends on the task and what happens if the system gets it wrong.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts patients’ and doctors’ adoption dynamics but does not state that patients have adopted AI faster.

r002.rationale: The response does not say physicians first learn about AI through patients who use it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think patients and doctors face very different tradeoffs. For a patient, the alternative to asking an AI a question often isn’t getting an immediate answer from a great doctor. It’s searching online, waiting for an appointment, or just sitting with uncertainty. So something that’s available immediately, explains things clearly, and lets you ask follow-up questions can be really valuable.

For doctors, the question is more demanding: Does this actually help me take better care of my patients? Does it fit into my workflow? How much time do I have to spend checking it? They’re responsible for what happens, so being impressed by an answer isn’t enough to justify relying on it.

And adoption doesn’t necessarily mean the same thing in those two settings. A patient might use AI to understand a diagnosis or prepare questions for a visit. A doctor might use it to draft a note or think through a difficult case. Those are different uses with different requirements for trust. I’d expect adoption to happen task by task, as people discover where the benefit is clear and where they still need human judgment.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts patients’ and doctors’ tradeoffs and possible uses, but does not state that patients have adopted AI faster than doctors.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that physicians often first learn about AI from patients who use it.
